chapter_theme: The dog Civakan gave the five padas is reborn a god, Sudanjanan, lord of the yakshas; he comes back, is recognised by a god's signs, thanks Civakan as his father and promises to come whenever he is remembered, while the narrator defends the transformation by alchemy's iron turned to gold and declares worship only for the destroyer of the eight karmas and release as the harvest of the tilled body. The city then plays at war in the pool of the water festival, and as the crowd streams home the musth elephant Asanivegam breaks loose.

cast.role: the hero, who gave the dying dog the five padas
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, now lord of the yakshas
the women of the city at the water festival
the young men of the city at the water festival
the warriors in the crowd returning from the festival
the musth state elephant that breaks loose

950.reading: The newly made god, lion-like, takes his delight among the celestial women with jewelled girdles, full breasts and lotus faces who have come to attend him.
950.event: The dog reborn as a god rejoices among the heavenly women who attend him.
950.nuance: The lion-like one is read as the reborn dog because 948-949 have just shown him appearing on a mountain top and the women of a golden palace gathering round; a reader coming to 950 alone might take the epithet for Civakan.

951.reading: The five padas he learned served as water to wash off his black karma; he became a god, shining like a rainbow in the sky, free of the pain of his broken body, and by avadhi knowledge he understood all that had befallen him.
951.event: The dying dog, having heard the five padas, is reborn a god and knows his former life.

claims.claim: hearing and holding the five sacred padas washes away dark karma and wins a god's birth
a god born in heaven knows his past state by clairvoyant knowledge (avadhi)

951.nuance: ஓதி here is the Jain avadhi, the knowledge of past and distant things given with a god's birth, not 'reciting'. The mantra does not end births: it turns the worst one into a better one, and the god still has a body and a station.

952.reading: As fire burns away iron's nature and makes it fine gold of its own colour, so the friend made him; longing for that dear friend, Sudanjanan with his bee-haunted garland swiftly appeared halting in the sky, it is said.
952.event: Sudanjanan comes down out of the sky to find Civakan, the friend who transformed him.
952.nuance: Civakan is the fire and the dog the iron: the image makes the teacher of the mantra, not the god it names, the agent of the change. என்பவே frames the arrival as told tradition.

953.reading: He appears with fragrant smoke spreading for a yojana around him, a body that glitters with moon-bright rays, a flawless jewelled crown hung with garlands, shining like the risen sun.
953.event: Sudanjanan appears before Civakan in a god's splendour.

954.reading: When the hill-shouldered one draws near, the prince sees that his long eyes do not blink, his body casts no shadow and his garland does not wilt, concludes that he is a god, and asks him, 'Sir, who are you?'
954.event: Civakan recognises the visitor as a god by his unblinking eyes, shadowless body and unfading garland, and asks who he is.
954.nuance: Civakan reads the god by three bodily signs before he speaks, so the recognition is an inference, not a revelation; the question then lets the god tell his own story.

955.reading: The god tells him that by his grace he went on and became lord of the yakshas, and now dwells on the summit of Chandrodaya on the conch-white mountain, and asks his 'father' to know it.
955.event: Sudanjanan tells Civakan he has become king of the yakshas on Mount Chandrodaya through Civakan's grace.
955.nuance: He calls the young man எந்தை, my father: the one who gave the mantra is the giver of his new birth.

956.reading: Hearing this, the patron of the gold-raining hand looks at him gladly and says that all the joy of the kingship held in the world of the conquerors has come to him today.
956.event: Civakan rejoices to learn what has become of the dog.
956.nuance: வென்றவர் உலகம் may be the heaven won by those who conquer by merit, or the world of the Jinas; either way Civakan counts another's rise as his own highest pleasure.

957.reading: Sudanjanan tells him that, like the lordship of the Bhagavan of the pindi tree where bees hum, he will now bring the whole world covered to his feet, and that whatever afflicts him will afflict the god as a mirror's image follows its object.
957.event: Sudanjanan promises Civakan the whole world at his feet and a share in every trouble.
957.nuance: The god measures what he offers by the Jina's sovereignty under the pindi (asoka) tree, so even the gift of the world is ranked below the Arhat's lordship. Line 4 (ஆடியுட் பாவை போல் நீ அணங்கியது அணங்க) is compressed and the sense of the mirror simile is a reading.

958.reading: He goes on: should warriors with swords gather and close round him at the elephant stalls and do violence, he need only think of his friend; Civakan is like the bond of intimacy that does not fall even when days and fortnights wane, and the god lacks nothing in this birth.
958.event: Sudanjanan tells Civakan to call him to mind if armed men ever besiege him.
958.nuance: The danger named, swordsmen closing round him by the elephant stalls, is the one the story is about to bring on: after Civakan masters the king's elephant he is seized and the god carries him off (patikam verse 15).

959.reading: The god, wearing jewels of sweet light, about to rise into the sky, embraces him with shoulders like golden bars, says 'Like your shadow I will not leave you; if trouble comes, think of me', and rises into the sky like a flash of lightning.
959.event: Sudanjanan embraces Civakan, promises to come when remembered, and goes back to the sky.
959.nuance: The promise binds the god's help to Civakan's remembering (நினைக்க): the help is summoned by thought, as the dog's rise was won by holding the padas in mind.

960.reading: The narrator tells the doubter not to ask whether this dog, with no good in it, could leave its body and be born a god of shining light: iron set in the smith's forge, blown upon and pierced with mercury becomes boundless red gold and takes the colour of fire.

claims.claim: even a creature with no merit can, by the mantra heard at death, be reborn a god

960.nuance: The narrator answers an objection before it is put: the image is alchemical, mercury (இரதம்) piercing iron in the forge, so the change is presented as a work of a known art, not a miracle. The figure of 952 returns, with the mantra now in the place of the friend's fire.

961.reading: Let the gods who revel on the hot breasts of the women, wounded by Kama's killing arrows, keep their glory; the speaker will bow his head to none but the one who removes the eight karmas that come as a garland and makes a sea of bliss.

claims.claim: worship belongs only to the one who has destroyed the eight karmas and gives bliss, not to gods who live in desire

961.nuance: The first-person refusal has no speech tag. It reads as the poet's own confession closing the episode; it could also be the reborn god's vow, since he has just been among the heavenly women (950). The gods are not denied; they are set aside as still subject to Kama.

962.reading: Yoke the plough of single-minded zeal, plough the field of the body, sow the red paddy of good vows, keep the water of conduct from failing and guard it with the fence of the five senses, and it will first yield the heavenly world and then the bliss of release of the conquerors.

claims.claim: zeal, vows, right conduct and guarded senses, worked on the body, yield heaven and then the release of the Jinas

962.nuance: The harvest comes in two crops: the gods' world is born (ஈன்று) on the way to the bliss of release, so heaven is a by-product, not the goal. Every stage is the practiser's own labour; no god tills the field.

963.reading: While these two part, the dark-eyed women and the young men, with a roar like that of those who churned the ocean round the planted Himalaya with the snake, go into the great pool crowded with swans to fight in play.
963.event: The townswomen and young men plunge into the great pool for the water festival.
963.nuance: The churning of the ocean is used only for its uproar; the poem pictures the mountain as the Himalaya.

964.reading: The pool is a bride whose fine garment is its mingling waves, whose two banks are her gold-girdled hips, whose lotus is her face and whose kuvalai are her eyes, and they enjoy her beauty.
964.event: The bathers take their pleasure in the pool.

965.reading: Striking the water hard and without stopping with fingers, palms and the backs of their hands so that it sounds like the tannumai, muzhavu, montai and takunicham drums, diving and playing, the young men with the bright-browed women are like the gods above.
965.event: The bathers drum on the water with their hands and dive and play.

966.reading: Spraying each other with syringes, flinging saffron, churning the honeyed water and chasing, laughing when the other side turns its back, binding garlands on the loser as a fine and taking tribute, they swim in pleasure; who can praise them in that flood of desire?
966.event: The bathers play at war in the water, routing one another and exacting garland-fines and tribute.
966.nuance: The vocabulary is a campaign's: புறங்கண்டு (seeing the back), தவறு (offence), திறை (tribute). The last line can be wonder at a joy past praising or a dry aside on people lost in a flood of desire; the Tamil allows both.

967.reading: Boats filled with sandal paste, boats of cool flower garlands, boats heaped with fine cloth and boats laden with jewels, pushed back and forth by the women and men, run and collide like ships on the waves.
967.event: The bathers drive little boats of paste, garlands, cloth and jewels at one another across the pool.

968.reading: Pearl strings swaying like water sprayed from a rutting elephant's trunk and their flower tufts tossing, the creeper-like women hurl balls filled with vermilion water, and the young men, glad to see them tire, fight on with desire.
968.event: The women pelt the men with balls of vermilion water and the men press the play as the women tire.

969.reading: The countless young men run with coloured powder, silks, garlands and paste and throw them at each other face to face, like lightning and stars fighting in the sky, and it surpasses the wedding the gods held on earth.
969.event: The young men pelt each other with powder, silk, garlands and paste.
969.nuance: Which wedding of the gods on earth is meant is not said.

970.reading: Rubbed butter, bright fragrant powder, ground sandal, musk and garlands foam on the water, swarms of strong-winged bees hum, the water is churned, and the pleasure passes its bounds.
970.nuance: இன்பம் இறந்ததே may mean that the pleasure exceeded all measure, as இறந்தது does in 969, or that the bathing pleasure came to its end; the next verse turns to dressing after the bath.

971.reading: The skilled young men, like gods worshipped with joined hands, with kaththigai garlands on their brows, all bring jewelled ornaments; the women, decked with pearls, their hair dried in perfumed smoke, their budding breasts bound in bodices and wound with jasmine strings, shine like creepers.
971.event: After the bath the women are dressed and adorned, and the young men bring them jewels.

972.reading: Fine gold chariots and red-gold palanquins jostle and tangle, dark elephants, horses and swift cow-elephants gather, warriors throng, and the whole crowd rises toward the guarded city like a flood from a tall mountain rushing to the dark sea.
972.event: The festival crowd, with chariots, palanquins, elephants and horses, streams back toward the city.

973.reading: Like the sea, like the wind, like fierce-eyed Death, like the thunderbolt with angry body, like the fire of the world's end, breaking the chained post at its root, appears the musth elephant Asanivegam, hard to overcome.
973.event: The musth elephant Asanivegam breaks its chained post and bursts out among the returning crowd.
973.nuance: The five similes run from nature (sea, wind) to Death and the end of the world; the elephant's name, Thunderbolt-speed, is held to the last word.

links.note: In 951 the dog, given the five padas at its ear as it died, is reborn a god; in 3036, in the last ilampakam, those lying at the point of death to whom the ascetic's words are set at the ear appear at once as unaging gods.
links.teaches: The single rescue of a dog becomes, at the end of the epic, a general working of the teacher's word, so the early episode is shown to be the model case of a rule the work states only at its close.

links.note: Both make a recited formula the agent of a change of state: Tirumular's சிவாயநம is an alchemist's pill that turns the body's cage to gold; the Cintamani's five padas are water that washes off black karma and bring a new god's body after death.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two mantras do different work: the Saiva syllables transmute the body the devotee already has through the Lord's act, while the Jain padas clear karma so that a better body follows in the next birth, with no Lord who acts.

gains.a: a Saiva counterpart in which the mantra changes this body rather than the next, which shows that 951's change comes only with death and a new birth
gains.b: a case in which the mantra works on one who cannot melt or contemplate, a dying animal, so that devotion of the mind is not what gives the formula its force

links.note: 952 has fire burn away iron's nature and turn it to gold, with Civakan as the fire; 960 repeats the forge, adds mercury piercing the iron, and uses it to answer the doubt that a dog could become a god.
links.teaches: The image moves from praising the friend as the cause of the change to defending the change itself as lawful, so the narrator relies on one figure first for gratitude and then for doctrine.

links.note: 959: the god promises to stay like Civakan's shadow and come if he thinks of him in trouble; patikam verse 15 tells how, when the king throws Civakan into prison, a god comes down the sky like lightning and carries him away.
links.teaches: The patikam's rescue is the promise of 959 kept, so the god's later appearance is not a chance intervention but the return of a debt owed for the mantra.

links.note: Both use iron turned to gold for a change of being: Tirumular says gold once made never turns back to iron, so one who has the guru's grace is not born again; the Cintamani's iron-to-gold is a dog reborn as a god.
links.teaches: The same alchemy marks a final release in Tirumular and only a rise within the round of births in the Cintamani, so the image's 'no return' belongs to the Saiva claim, not to the figure itself.

gains.a: a reading of its own image as a step and not an end, since the god of 951 is still embodied
gains.b: an instance where the gold is a higher birth, which shows that the couplet's finality is a doctrinal addition to the metallurgy

links.note: Tirumular says those who grieve the ascetics who taught the mantra are born as dogs (சுணங்கன்); the Cintamani's dog (சுணங்கன்) is raised to a god's birth by the mantra heard from Civakan.
links.teaches: Read together, the teacher's mantra decides birth in both directions: offending its teachers sinks a man to a dog, and receiving it lifts a dog to a god, so the same word names the bottom of the scale in both books.

gains.a: the Saiva warning that the dog's birth is itself the fruit of offending the bearers of the mantra, which deepens the narrator's 'no good in it'
gains.b: a story in which the same creature climbs back up the scale by the same means that, in the couplet, cast men down

links.note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities (எண்குணத்தான்) is useless; 961 vows to bow the head to no one but the one who removes the eight karmas (எண்வினை) and gives bliss, and sets aside the gods of desire.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's positive command into an exclusion and fills its unexplained 'eight' with a count of karmas destroyed, so the Kural's open epithet is given a Jain content it does not itself state.

gains.a: a canonical model, the bowing head of the Kural's first chapter, for its refusal
gains.b: one reading of its undefined eight, together with the inference that the bow must be withheld from other gods

links.note: Kural 24: one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness is a seed for the finest ground; 962 builds the whole farm, with zeal as the plough, the body as the field, vows as seed, conduct as water and the five senses as the fence.
links.teaches: The couplet's one image of the guarded self as seed is spelled out as a season of tillage, and its unnamed 'finest ground' gets two harvests, heaven first and release after.

gains.a: a classical root for its allegory, in which the guarding of the five senses already leads to the best place
gains.b: an answer to what வரன் yields, given as a sequence of heaven and release, and a place for vows and conduct beside the guarding of the senses

links.note: In 962 the practiser yokes the plough, tills his own body and guards it with the senses' fence until release ripens; in Tirumular 1875 the first Lord has taken the poet's soul as his field to plough, and praise and blame fall away.
links.teaches: The two pictures of the tilled self disagree on who holds the plough: in the Jain allegory release is the crop of one's own labour, in Tirumular the Lord does the tilling, so the shared farm figure carries the dispute between release by effort and release by grace.

gains.a: a Saiva counter-picture that brings out how wholly 962 leaves the work to the practiser, with no god in the field
gains.b: the Jain alternative it implicitly answers, which makes its passive 'he has taken my soul to plough' a claim about grace and not only an image

links.note: Paripadal 6 sets the river play out as a battle array, with bathers drilling rivalry 'as in war' and carrying syringes (சிவிறியர்); in 966 the bathers spray with syringes (சிவிறி) and the play goes through a campaign's whole course, the enemy's back seen, the offender fined with garlands, tribute taken.
links.teaches: The Sangam festival's figure of water-play as battle is carried by the epic from the array to the victory and its exactions, and set just before a real terror breaks out (973), so the mock war of desire gives way to a true danger.

gains.a: the Sangam convention of the festival as a war of pleasure, which explains why the verse reaches for rout and tribute
gains.b: a later use of the convention that completes the war figure with conquest and penalty, which the Paripadal's arrays only begin

links.note: Patikam verse 14 tells that on the same day the hero gave nectar to the dying dog at the bathing festival, he overcame the victorious elephant that had terrified Gunamalai; 973 is the elephant breaking loose as the festival crowd returns.
links.teaches: The patikam binds the mercy to the dog and the mastery of the elephant as one day's deeds, so the chapter's turn from the god's farewell through the water-play to the rampaging tusker is a single day planned as a pair of the hero's virtues.

new_concepts.gloss: the gods as a class of embodied beings in the round of births, ranked and numbered beside humans, animals and hell-beings
new_concepts.label_source: verse 951 uses தேவன், 960 தேவன், 961 தேவர்; id as used in the Neelakesi marks

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
new_concepts.label_source: verse 962 uses விரதம்; id as used in earlier Cintamani marks

new_concepts.gloss: water-play in the river or pool, especially the festival bathing of the town and of lovers in the new flood
new_concepts.label_source: label mine for the scene of 963-970 (பொய்கை புக்கார், குடைந்தும் ஆடி); id as used in the Paripadal and Cintamani marks

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: verse 965 names the drums (தண்ணுமை முழவு மொந்தை தகுணிச்சம்) and ஓசை; id as used in earlier marks

new_concepts.gloss: the wedding; the rite that makes a marriage
new_concepts.label_source: verse 969 uses மன்றல்; id as used in earlier Cintamani marks

source_issues: Verse 958 line 4 prints an unmatched parenthesis in 'பிறவி (னென்றான்.'; the reading குறைவிலன் பிறவின் is uncertain.
Verses 951, 954-956, 959, 962-969 and 972 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 963 line 4 'மொய்த்திரள வன்ன' is hard to divide (மொய்த்து இரள் அன்னம்?); verse 957 line 4 (ஆடியுட் பாவை போனீ யணங்கிய தணங்க) is compressed and hard to construe.
